paras: The beating and expulsion of Jim Cherry took place at Sulphur Springs, Texas, in August 1905, when citizens beat Cherry, a Black man, over a remark about a young white woman and ordered him out of town. According to the wire account, the citizens first debated whether to lynch him, and he left town in a covered wagon. The incident was reported as an aftermath of the burning of Tom Williams at Sulphur Springs, in which the same woman was the alleged victim.

The Jefferson Jimplecute reported that on the previous Friday, August 11, "several thousand citizens" burned a Black man named Tom Williams on the Sulphur Springs square on the charge of attempting to assault Miss Nettie Griggs, a young white woman, a mile outside town.

In a dispatch dated August 12, Jim Cherry, described as "a yellow negro," was said to have made "a derogatory statement concerning the character" of Miss Griggs. He was beaten, and citizens then held "a consultation" on "whether or not to lynch him." Instead he was ordered to leave town, which he did in a covered wagon.
The Jefferson Jimplecute gave a shorter version, saying Cherry had made "an insulting remark about the young girl" and was attacked by "several citizens," beaten and ordered to leave "right away."
No report of arrests, an inquiry or any official response to the beating appears in the coverage, and Cherry's later whereabouts are not reported.

The Bryan Morning Eagle ran the dispatch on August 13 under the headlines "Jim Cherry Beaten" and "Negro Who Made Derogatory Remarks Had Narrow Escape." The Palestine Daily Herald reprinted the same text the next day with an August 14 dateline. The Jimplecute, a weekly, added the incident as a single sentence to its account of the burning on August 19.
None of the white papers commented on the attackers, and the wire headline treated the beating as an escape from lynching.

reader.title: Beating and expulsion of Jim Cherry
bases: Citizens beat Cherry and ordered him out of town after debating whether to lynch him; he was not killed (A3, A5).

The Sulphur Springs wire dispatch (A3, reprinted A4) and the Jefferson Jimplecute's differently worded brief (A5), whose Williams details also differ from the wire, agree that Cherry was beaten and ordered to leave over a remark about Miss Griggs; only the wire reports the lynching consultation.

accounts.label: Sulphur Springs wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Cherry made a derogatory statement about Miss Griggs's character, was beaten, citizens consulted whether to lynch him, and he was ordered out and left in a covered wagon.

accounts.label: Jefferson Jimplecute brief
accounts.gist: Cherry made an insulting remark about the young girl, was attacked and beaten by several citizens and ordered to leave the city at once; no lynching consultation or wagon is mentioned.

framing.detail: The wire headline 'Negro Who Made Derogatory Remarks Had Narrow Escape' presented the beating as a lesser outcome than lynching, without comment on the attackers.
The Jimplecute reported the beating in one sentence appended to its account of the burning, without comment.

versions.value: Beaten, lynching debated by citizens, ordered out, left in covered wagon
Beaten by several citizens and ordered to leave right away; no lynching consultation mentioned

conflicts.note: The Jimplecute omits rather than denies the consultation; the wire is the fuller and earlier report.
A4 was printed on Aug. 14, so its dateline likely reflects the reprinting date; the Aug. 12 dateline in the Aug. 13 paper is the better evidence.

set_aside: Editorial 'Is It Possible?' on the Texas Negro Baptist convention and the burning of Tom Williams; does not mention Cherry (issue date appears earlier than the burning it discusses).
'More Particulars': Sulphur Springs dispatch on the alleged attempted assault on Miss Nettie Griggs by Tom Williams, who was burned on the square; no mention of Cherry.
'Colored Baptists Endorse Mob Law': reprinted Portland Advocate item on the Williams burning and the Baptist convention; no mention of Cherry.
